claims.text: A machine-learning framework can separately predict lattice and electronic thermal conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed framework will reduce total-thermal-conductivity predictive error by approximately 30–50% relative to Debye-based or defect-free bulk models.
The proposed framework will accurately capture atomic-scale disorder and oxygen-induced modifications in HfNbTaTiZr.
The study considers pristine HfNbTaTiZr and HfNbTaTiZr containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
Local force-constant distributions can be used to compute the lattice contribution to thermal conductivity.
DFT-derived electronic descriptors can be used to compute the electronic thermal conductivity.
Ab initio molecular dynamics can supply training or calibration data for a machine-learned thermal-transport model.
Inelastic-scattering data can calibrate the proposed model's temperature-dependent effects in HfNbTaTiZr.
Below 200 K, the lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr are comparable.
HfNbTaTiZr containing 1 wt.% oxygen has a total thermal conductivity of 10–17 W/(m K) between 300 and 1200 K.
Local atomic disorder causes variations in force constants that affect lattice heat transport.
Oxygen impurities modify electron-phonon coupling and thereby affect the separate lattice and electronic transport channels.

Separating lattice and electronic transport and representing local disorder, impurity effects, and temperature-dependent electron-phonon interactions will improve physical accuracy over approaches that conflate the channels.
The model's total-conductivity predictions will quantitatively agree with low-temperature heat-capacity and high-temperature conductivity measurements.
Existing Debye-based or perfect-crystal approaches omit lattice disorder and oxygen-impurity effects in this alloy.
Existing approaches show larger discrepancies with both low- and high-temperature measurements than the proposed model will show.
Electrical and thermal transport measurements have been reported from 4 to 300 K, and the Wiedemann–Franz relationship has been used to estimate phonon and electron contributions.
Prior work has trained machine-learned force fields using ab initio molecular dynamics and then used Green–Kubo calculations to derive thermal conductivity.

A PbSnTeSe high-entropy-alloy study combined special quasirandom structures, DFT, Boltzmann transport, and Green–Kubo theory and calculated electronic thermal conductivity from DFT-derived electronic states.
Failure to reduce predictive error by at least 30%, or disagreement of the predicted channel contributions with independent measurements beyond experimental uncertainty, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The initial state and falsification design include pristine, nominally oxygen-free HfNbTaTiZr, whereas the boundary says predictions are applicable only for oxygen levels around 1 wt.%, leaving the claimed applicability to the pristine control internally inconsistent.
